title: Efficient calculation of real-space lattice propagators in the presence of a Fermi sea
abstract: We present an efficient method for computing the real-space propagators (lattice Green's functions) of any tight-binding Hamiltonian in the presence of a Fermi sea with carrier concentration $x$. The method is valid for any lattice, dispersion, and dimension, provided the corresponding $x=0$ propagators are known. We show that suitable combinations of the finite-$x$ particle-addition propagators have a real or imaginary part trivially related to their $x=0$ counterpart, while the remaining part follows from a Kramers-Kronig relation that can be evaluated for all energies at once using the fast Fourier transforms. The computational cost is therefore independent of the dimensionality, unlike that of direct Brillouin-zone integration. The particle-removal propagators follow from general identities. We validate the method against direct integration for hypercubic lattices in one, two, and three dimensions, and use the 2D square lattice to illustrate how the shape of the Fermi surface is imprinted on the spatial structure of the propagators. In particular, at energies far outside the band, the propagator maps converge to the Fraunhofer diffraction pattern whose aperture is the unoccupied part of the Brillouin zone.
summary: This paper presents an efficient, dimension-agnostic method to calculate real-space lattice Green's functions for doped tight-binding models. By leveraging Kramers-Kronig relations and FFTs, the authors bypass the computational bottleneck of direct Brillouin-zone integration. The results demonstrate that the spatial decay and structure of the propagator directly encode the geometry of the Fermi surface.
main_problem: The paper develops an efficient theoretical method to calculate real-space lattice propagators (Green's functions) for a tight-binding model when the system is doped, i.e., in the presence of a Fermi sea.
main_result: The method achieves a computational cost independent of the lattice dimensionality by utilizing Kramers-Kronig relations evaluated via FFTs, allowing the mapping of Fermi surface geometry onto the spatial structure of the propagators.
method: The core technique involves relating the finite-$x$ propagators to the $x=0$ case using known identities and then employing Kramers-Kronig relations, which are efficiently computed for all energies simultaneously using Fast Fourier Transforms.
model_or_system: The model is a non-interacting, tight-binding Hamiltonian defined on an arbitrary lattice, characterized by a Fermi sea determined by the carrier concentration $x$. The calculation focuses on the particle-addition part of the lattice Green's function.
key_observables: Real-space lattice propagators ($G_n(z; x)$), the real and imaginary parts of the propagator, and the resulting diffraction patterns.
important_parameters: Carrier concentration ($x$), Fermi energy ($E_F$), lattice distance ($n$), and energy ($\omega$).
main_assumptions: The method is valid for any lattice and dispersion, provided the $x=0$ propagators are known, and it is derived in the limit of zero broadening ($\eta 	o 0$).
figures_summary: Figures compare the proposed method against direct integration across 1D, 2D, and 3D lattices. Maps illustrate how the Fermi surface geometry (e.g., circular vs. square) imprints itself on the spatial structure of the propagator magnitude and sign.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, derives the necessary identities relating finite-$x$ propagators to $x=0$ counterparts, details the use of Kramers-Kronig relations via FFTs, and validates the method by comparing results across various dimensions and doping levels.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, dimension-independent computational tool for studying electronic structure in doped solids, which is highly relevant for understanding transport and correlation effects in materials science.
